opus-5.5.text:
I think they're going to coexist for quite a while, because they're really solving different problems. Interactive tools, where you're in the editor and the model is completing your code or you're chatting with it about a function, are great when you know roughly what you want and you're steering in real time. The human stays in the loop at every step, and that's valuable when the task is ambiguous or you're still figuring out the design.

Background agents are a different mode. You hand off a well-scoped task, like fix this bug, write tests for this module, or migrate this API, and you come back later to review a pull request. That's much closer to delegating to a colleague than to using a tool. As models get more reliable over longer horizons, more work moves into that bucket.

What I expect is that the boundary keeps shifting. Things that today need tight interactive supervision will become delegable as reliability improves. But I don't think interactive use goes away, because the frontier of what's hard keeps moving too. Engineers will spend more of their time on specification and review: deciding what should be built, breaking it into pieces an agent can handle, and checking the output. The interactive tools become the place where you do the thinking, and the background agents become the place where the execution happens.

The interesting question is the handoff between them. You want to start interactively, realize this is a chunk you can delegate, kick it off in the background, and then pull the result back into your interactive session to review and refine. The products that get that workflow right, where moving between the two modes is seamless, are the ones I think will win.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly predicts that the two modes will “coexist for quite a while,” describing interactive IDE use and background agents as distinct approaches.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they coexist for a while, and then the balance shifts pretty decisively toward the background agents. But the interactive tools don't go away, because they're serving a different function.

The way I'd frame it: the interactive tool is where you're thinking. You're in the editor, you have a half-formed idea, and the model is a very fast collaborator who helps you figure out what you actually want. The latency matters there, the tight loop matters, because you're using the tool to shape your own intent. You don't know the spec yet. You're discovering it.

The background agent is where you've already decided. You know what you want, you can write it down in a paragraph or a ticket, and you don't want to sit there and watch it happen. You hand it off, go do something else, and come back to a pull request. That's a fundamentally different relationship. It's closer to delegating to a colleague than to using a tool.

So the question of how they coexist is really a question of how much of software work is "I know what I want" versus "I'm figuring out what I want." And right now, honestly, a lot of the work that gets done interactively is work that could have been handed off, except people don't trust the agent enough yet, or the agent isn't reliable enough yet on that class of task. As reliability goes up, that work migrates to the background. The interactive surface shrinks down to the genuinely exploratory stuff, which is the most interesting part anyway.

What I expect to see is the interactive tools becoming more like a cockpit for the background agents. You're not typing code with autocomplete, you're reviewing five agents' work, redirecting one of them, pulling one problem back into the foreground because it needs your judgment. The editor becomes the place where you supervise rather than the place where you produce.

And I think the people who are going to be very good at this are the ones who get comfortable writing down what they want clearly enough that a background agent can run with it. That's a skill. It's close to being a good engineering manager, actually. The interactive mode lets you be sloppy, because you correct as you go. The background mode rewards being precise up front. Both are going to exist, but I'd bet on the second one being where most of the leverage ends up.

r001.rationale: The response says the interactive tools and background agents “coexist for a while,” directly predicting prolonged coexistence.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary. When you’re figuring out what you want to build, you want a very interactive experience. You make a change, look at the result, and say, “Actually, that’s not quite what I meant. Let’s try this.” That fast feedback loop helps you figure out the problem as much as solve it.

Once you have a task that’s well defined, you’d rather hand it off to an agent and let it work in the background. You can keep working on something else, then come back and review what it did.

So I’d expect people to move between those modes. You might start interactively, send a few tasks off to background agents, and then pull one back into an interactive session when it needs your judgment. The interesting part is making that handoff feel natural.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that interactive coding and background agents will complement each other and describes switching between them, but it does not say they will coexist for a prolonged period.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re complementary. Sometimes you know exactly what you want, and you want to work interactively with the model, look at the result, and steer it. Other times, you have a well-defined task that you’d rather hand off and come back to when it’s done.

And you’ll move between those modes. You might start interactively to figure out the right approach, send an agent off to implement it, and then come back together to review the changes. The interesting question is how smoothly you can make that transition—how much context the agent carries with it, and when it knows to ask for your input.

So I don’t think one replaces the other. As the agents get better, you’ll delegate larger pieces of work, but you’ll still want that tight feedback loop when you’re exploring or making important decisions.

r001.rationale: The response says interactive work and agent delegation are complementary and that one will not replace the other; it also expects users to keep using interactive feedback as agents improve, conveying ongoing coexistence.
